newsitem.title: USA: Mexico's Ortiz sees 4 pct GDP growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Ortiz sees 4 pct GDP growth in 1997.

text.p: Mexican Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz said Sunday that he expects Mexico's Gross Domestic Product would grow by about four percent next year.

"In Mexico, analysts' predictions exceed four percent. We think it is possible, but we prefer to be conservative," Ortiz said at a conference on the fringes of the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.
Mexico's economy is expected to grow by about 3.5 percent this year, climbing back from a 6.9 percent contraction in 1995.

Ortiz told an audience of international bankers attending a conference of the Institute of International Finance that he expected Mexico's inflation to fall to about 15 or 16 percent next year from around 25 percent this year.
Ortiz said that he believed that Mexico's export-led recovery was sustainable, pointing out that small- and medium-size firms are increasingly becoming involved in export activities.
Up to now, he said, about 500 companies were responsible for about 80 percent of Mexico's exports.
Ortiz added that the "maquiladora" industries, which traditionally brought around 90 percent of their inputs from abroad, are starting to turn to small Mexican suppliers.
Regarding investment in sectors dominated by the state such as the petrochemical and infrastructure industries, Ortiz predicted that there would be greater private sector involvement in 1997.

Another key reform, he said, was the overhauling of Mexico's social security system. As of next year, all existing pensions will be paid out of the government budget, while workers' contributions will go into funds run by private sector managers.
"This will be the first time Mexico will have a long-term capital market," Ortiz said.
Ortiz said that the cost of paying for pensions and the bailout of troubled Mexican banks would probably result in a "small fiscal deficit of less than one percent of GDP."
However, he said he would continue to push for increased government savings in order to keep that shortfall below one percentage point of GDP.
He said he expected next year's current account of the balance of payments to show a deficit of less than two percent.
